doc.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Trust and spontaneity in the duo
summary: She tells Cameron not to be shocked when she changes things; he describes letting go of responsibility and trusting her and the repertoire more as the partnership matured.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I always tell him, “Don‟t be shocked.” Sometimes he‟ll go… Brown, C.: I‟m shocked. I‟m always shocked.
Like sometimes he‟ll go, “What‟s goin‟on here?” And I always says, “Don‟t get shocked. Just if, when in doubt, lay out. It‟s okay. I know where I… I know what‟s happening

„cause an idea will come and he tries… you know, he‟s cool. He, he‟s trusts me. But at first, he‟s like, ooo, where is she going with this one?” [laughs] So it‟s not really set. We have a, we have a beginning usually and an ending, I‟d say. But in the middle, anything can happen, you know. Brown, C.: Well, I think that‟s been fun lately, as the band, as our relationship matures musically.
Uh-huh. Brown, C.: I mean, I think for me, for quite a while, it was feeling like there was a lot of, a lot of responsibility on my shoulders and…
Yeah. Brown, C.: …to kinda keep everything glued together and…
[laughs] Brown, C.: …now I‟m kinda letting that go.
Yeah. [laughs] Brown, C.: And just trusting her more.
Yeah. Brown, C.: And just, uh, let‟s be free. Let‟s see what happens.
Yeah. He… Brown, C.: And it‟s more fun in a way. I‟d say [stammers].
Yeah. Uh-huh. Brown, C.: And so we‟re more trusting of each other and, and of the repertoire.
Yeah. Brown, C.: And seeing where it takes us.
